analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that block workers from taking a new job, enforced by the FTC and Labor Department.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban most noncompete agreements was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to require most workers to sign noncompete agreements, which bar a worker from taking a similar job with a competitor after leaving. Economists cited in the bill estimate one in five American workers is covered by one. It keeps narrow exceptions for people selling a business or leaving a partnership, leaves trade-secret and confidentiality agreements untouched, and gives the Federal Trade Commission and the Labor Department power to investigate and fine violators, with a private right of action for workers.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one in five American workers covered by a noncompete agreement, who the bill's findings say currently face lower wages, blocked job moves, and pressure to idle or leave their field entirely. Workers would be able to change jobs, negotiate, or start a competing business without facing a lawsuit.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits entering, enforcing, or threatening to enforce a noncompete agreement with any worker covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, and voids existing such agreements going forward.

Relies on the bill's finding that noncompete agreements reduce wages, restrict worker mobility, and slow innovation, while employers already have narrower tools like trade secrets, intellectual property protections, and nondisclosure agreements.
Lets workers sue for actual damages plus attorney's fees, and lets the Labor Department impose a civil fine of up to $5,000 per week of violation, paid to the aggrieved worker.
Requires employers to post a notice of the ban in the workplace and authorizes the Labor Secretary to run a public awareness campaign.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements to hold onto trained staff, limit poaching, and keep wages down lose that tool. They would have to compete on pay and conditions or use narrower, existing protections like nondisclosure agreements.

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose a tool for protecting investments in training and proprietary customer relationships; the bill answers this by leaving trade secrets, IP protections, and nondisclosure agreements fully intact, but some firms would still face more worker departures.

The bill preserves an exception letting business sellers and senior executives with severance agreements sign noncompetes lasting up to a year, so the practice survives at the top of companies even as it is banned for rank-and-file workers.
Enforcement depends largely on workers themselves filing complaints or lawsuits against a current or former employer, which many workers will be reluctant to do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain — restoring job mobility and bargaining power for an estimated one in five workers — is large, and the bill shields employers' genuine trade-secret and confidentiality interests rather than abolishing all restrictive agreements. The executive carve-out is a real compromise that leaves a class-based double standard in place. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs for working people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the two House committees it was referred to and the subcommittee it was sent to; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA) introduced the bill on February 25, 2021, joined from the start by Reps. Mike Gallagher (R-WI), Anna Eshoo (D-CA), and Peter Meijer (R-MI).
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee on the day of introduction.
On February 26, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
The bill gained six cosponsors in total, split between two Republicans and four Democrats, but no further action was ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on noncompete agreements are better off, because the ban never advanced and they kept the ability to bind workers to them.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with Republican original cosponsors, and its six cosponsors split two Republicans and four Democrats; it died in committee without ever facing a vote.

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompete agreements (across service, staffing, healthcare, and tech sectors)
industries.note: The bill strips them of the power to stop departing workers from joining competitors, which its findings say suppresses wages and traps roughly one in five workers. Their interest in keeping the tool runs directly against workers' interest in mobility and pay.

industries.industry: Business sellers and senior executives of companies being acquired
industries.note: The bill carves them out: they may still sign noncompete agreements in connection with selling a business, capped at one year for executives with severance packages, preserving a practice banned for ordinary workers.

industries.industry: Employers relying on trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements
industries.note: The bill explicitly leaves trade-secret protections, intellectual property law, and nondisclosure agreements in place, making them the surviving, narrower channel for protecting confidential information and customer lists.
